How We Cut Our CI Build Times in Half

By Priya Raman · March 14, 2026

Tweet Share

Twelve months ago, a clean build of our main repository took forty-one minutes on CI. Engineers had learned to push a change, go to lunch, and hope. This post walks through what we changed, in the order we changed it, and how much each step actually bought us.

The short version: remote caching gave us the biggest single win, test sharding the second, and a handful of boring fixes to our Docker layers made up the rest. None of it was magic, but the combination took the median pipeline from forty-one minutes down to nineteen.

Measuring before optimizing

Before touching anything, we exported six weeks of pipeline timings into a spreadsheet and grouped them by stage. It turned out that compilation was only a third of the wall-clock time; the rest was split between dependency installation, container image builds, and a long tail of flaky integration tests that were retried automatically.

We also discovered that a single integration suite, the one exercising the billing service, accounted for almost nine minutes on its own because it spun up a fresh database for every test case.

Remote caching

Our build tool already supported a content-addressed cache, but it was only enabled on developer laptops. Turning on a shared remote cache for CI meant that most pull requests only rebuilt the handful of targets they actually touched. We wrote up the configuration in our internal guide, and the relevant flags are documented in the upstream manual.

The cache hit rate on the first day was 83 percent. By the end of the week it had settled at 91 percent, and the compile stage dropped from fourteen minutes to under three.

Sharding the slow suites

Next, we split the billing integration suite across four parallel runners and replaced the per-test database with transactions that roll back at the end of each case. That alone saved seven minutes, and it had the pleasant side effect of making the suite deterministic enough that we could turn off automatic retries.

ci:
  billing-tests:
    parallelism: 4
    command: make test-billing SHARD=$CI_NODE_INDEX

Finally, we reordered our Dockerfile so that dependency manifests are copied and installed before the application source. A change to a single source file no longer invalidates the dependency layer, which saves another four to five minutes on most runs.

If you want to try the same approach, start with measurement. The biggest wins were not where we expected them, and without the data we would have spent weeks tuning the compiler flags instead.
